# Job 28 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

## Overview & Authorship Question

**Who speaks this chapter?** This is debated. The traditional view (and the one most commentators adopt) is that Job himself speaks it. Ellicott notes that “the difficulty to the ordinary reader is in not perceiving that the person spoken of in Job 28:3 is man, and not God” — yet it is Job drawing a magnificent contrast between human ingenuity and divine wisdom. [Ellicott, v.1](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/job/28.htm)

However, Enduring Word (Guzik) reports that “most scholars find it impossible to believe that Job ever recited this poem,” because its calm, reflective tone seems so different from the surrounding speeches. Some propose it is an interlude by the narrator of the book. Guzik favours the simpler solution: “Why should it surprise us if Job, having exhausted all other avenues of protest and inquiry, should all at once slip quietly into a more reflective mood?” [Enduring Word](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-28/)

Gill explains the chapter’s overall design: either to show the folly of those who diligently pursue earthly things while neglecting true wisdom, or “rather to observe, that though things the most secret … hidden in the bowels of the earth, may be investigated … by the sagacity and diligence of men, yet wisdom cannot.” [Gill, Introduction](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/job/28.htm)

The Pulpit Commentary sees the chapter as Job concluding that “God is incomprehensible by man and inscrutable; and that it is only given to man to know him sufficiently for his practical guidance.” [Pulpit, vv.1-28](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/28.htm)

---

## Part 1: Man’s Mining Triumphs (vv.1–11)

**v. 1 — “Surely there is a mine for silver and a place where gold is refined.”**

Job opens by describing how men search out precious metals. Gill notes that silver is mentioned first possibly because it was the earliest metal in use — “we read of pieces of silver, or shekels of silver, in the times of Abraham, but not of any golden coin.” The Hebrew word for silver comes from a root meaning “desire,” because it is so desirable to men. Gold, by contrast, gets its Hebrew name from its yellow colour. [Gill, v.1](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/job/28.htm)

The Pulpit Commentary notes that Asia itself was probably the source of silver in primitive times; gold was especially abundant in Arabia, so Job would have been familiar with refining processes. [Pulpit, v.1](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/28.htm)

**v. 2 — “Iron is taken from the earth, and copper is smelted from ore.”**

Gill observes that iron is “nearer the surface of the earth” and “taken out of the dust” — more common and easier to obtain. Copper (or brass) is “molten out of the stone” — extracted from ore by smelting. He notes that Tubal-Cain (Genesis 4:22) was the first instructor in working brass and iron. [Gill, v.2](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/job/28.htm)

The Pulpit Commentary clarifies that “brass” here means copper, since the amalgam brass is never found in a natural state. Copper was yielded abundantly from mines worked by the Egyptians in the Sinaitic peninsula. [Pulpit, v.2](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/28.htm)

**v. 3 — “Man puts an end to the darkness; he probes the farthest recesses for ore in deepest darkness.”**

Ellicott makes the crucial point here: *this is man, not God*. “Man setteth an end to darkness, and searcheth out to the furthest bound the stones of darkness and the shadow of death.” [Ellicott, v.3](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/job/28.htm)

Gill explains: the miner, by opening a shaft, “lets in natural light, or carries artificial light along with him, and so puts an end to the darkness which had reigned there before, even from the creation.” He applies this spiritually: “so spiritual miners, that search into the mines of the Scriptures, should not be discouraged with darkness and difficulties that may attend their search.” [Gill, v.3](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/job/28.htm)

The Pulpit Commentary: “The miner’s first operation is to pierce the ground with a shaft … Through this the light enters into what was previously pitch darkness.” [Pulpit, v.3](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/28.htm)

**v. 4 — “Far from human habitation he cuts a shaft in places forgotten by the foot of man. Far from men he dangles and sways.”**

The Pulpit Commentary explains the obscure original: “He breaketh open a shaft, away from where men inhabit … they hang swinging to and fro far from men. The descent of the shaft is made by a rope, to which they ‘hang swinging’ all the time that they descend.” The miner seeks secrecy, working “far from the haunts of men.” [Pulpit, v.4](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/28.htm)

Ellicott offers an alternative rendering: “Man breaketh open a shaft where none sojourneth; they are forgotten where none passeth by … they hang afar from the haunts of men, they flit to and fro.” Or alternatively, the floodwaters that break out are drained and dried up by man’s engineering, so completely that “those who walk over the place forget that it was once a river.” [Ellicott, v.4](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/job/28.htm)

Gill’s version: the miner may be called an “inhabitant” of the mine, but when a flood of water arises (a common danger in mines), he must flee. Then by “engines, pumps, and buckets” the waters are drawn up and cleared so work can resume. [Gill, v.4](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/job/28.htm)

Enduring Word comments: “Those forgotten could be explorers far from home, or slaves in the mine” (citing Andersen). The verse highlights both the danger and the isolation of the miner’s work. [Enduring Word](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-28/)

**v. 5 — “Food may come from the earth, but from below it is transformed as by fire.”**

Gill explains: “out of it cometh bread” — wheat cast into the earth rises and produces grain, which when ground makes bread. “Under it is turned up as it were fire” refers to coal or sulphureous matter dug from beneath the same surface that grows bread. Some think it means precious stones that “glitter and sparkle like fire.” [Gill, v.5](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/job/28.htm)

The Pulpit Commentary: man’s cleverness turns the earth to various uses. By tillage of its surface, it produces bread; by mining operations, “the under part of it is turned up as by fire” — fire being used in some ancient mining processes to detach masses of material (citing Pliny). [Pulpit, v.5](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/28.htm)

Ellicott paints a vivid picture: “While the ploughman and the reaper till and gather the fruits of the earth on its surface, the miner far below maintains perpetual fires, as also does the volcanic mountain, with its fields and vineyards luxuriant and fertile on its sides.” [Ellicott, v.5](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/job/28.htm)

Enduring Word quotes Bradley: “Above spreads the surface of mother earth, with her waving cornfields, rich with human sustenance. Below, her very entrails are torn and devastated as by flames.” [Enduring Word](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-28/)

**v. 6 — “Its rocks are the source of sapphires, containing flecks of gold.”**

Gill notes that in some parts of the earth “its stones are a quarry of sapphires” — the sapphire being a sky-coloured stone with golden specks, one of the stones in the high priest’s breastplate (Exodus 24:10). The “dust of gold” suggests either gold as plentiful as dust or the golden specks within sapphires (as Pliny described). [Gill, v.6](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/job/28.htm)

The Pulpit Commentary observes that the Hebrew *sappir* may be lapis lazuli rather than the modern sapphire. The gold is “commonly scattered in such specks” in auriferous rocks. [Pulpit, v.6](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/28.htm)

Ellicott: “So ingenious is man that he discovereth a place of which the stones are sapphires and the very dust gold.” [Ellicott, v.6](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/job/28.htm)

**v. 7 — “No bird of prey knows that path; no falcon’s eye has seen it.”**

Gill explains: the “path” is the path made by miners to the gold and silver ores. The eagle (some render it “the vulture”) is the most sharp-sighted of birds, yet “it never could look into the bowels of the earth, or discover a track leading thereunto.” He applies it spiritually to “the paths of God in providence, which are unsearchable and past finding out.” [Gill, v.7](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/job/28.htm)

The Pulpit Commentary: “The miner’s path through the bowels of the earth … the vulture is probably the most keen-sighted of birds, but it cannot even get a glimpse of the subterraneous path.” [Pulpit, v.7](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/28.htm)

Enduring Word (citing Andersen): “The falcon is celebrated for its vision, the lion for its courage. But neither is as observant or as intrepid as man.” [Enduring Word](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-28/)

**v. 8 — “Proud beasts have never trodden it; no lion has ever prowled over it.”**

Gill renders “the lion’s whelps” as “the children of pride” (as also in Job 41:34), applying it spiritually to self-righteous persons who “are proud boasters of themselves.” These “never trod the way of holiness, nor walked in the path of truth.” [Gill, v.8](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/job/28.htm)

The Pulpit Commentary: wild beasts “would haunt the mountains and penetrate into natural caverns, but would never adventure themselves in the shafts and adits of miners.” [Pulpit, v.8](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/28.htm)

**v. 9 — “The miner strikes the flint; he overturns mountains at their base.”**

Gill: the miner, meeting with rock or flint, “is not discouraged, but goes to work therewith, and with his hammer in his hand lays upon the rock … and beats it to pieces.” Some interpreters (Jarchi, Aben Ezra) understand this and the following verses of God, not man — but “the former sense is best, and most agreeable to the context.” [Gill, v.9](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/job/28.htm)

The Pulpit Commentary cites Herodotus, who described Phoenician mining at Thasos where “a huge mountain has been turned upside down in the search for ores,” and Pliny, who records that Spanish miners would undercut a mountain with wedges, then destroy the supports so “the mountain falls in upon itself with a crash that cannot be imagined.” [Pulpit, v.9](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/28.htm)

**v. 10 — “He hews out channels in the rocks, and his eyes spot every treasure.”**

The Pulpit Commentary explains that this likely refers to tunnels or ducts constructed in mines to carry off subterranean water. “Nothing escapes his notice. Even as he constructs these ducts he has his eye open to note any signs of mineral wealth.” [Pulpit, v.10](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/28.htm)

Gill: the miner cleaves rocks to find things of value, and by cutting his way opens courses for water to drain away from the mine, so he can continue working. His eye “seeth every precious thing” — gold, silver, or precious stones in the cliffs. [Gill, v.10](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/job/28.htm)

Ellicott describes the process as “tunnelling and excavating, and that of making canals and lining them with stone; and in the course of such works many precious things would be discovered.” [Ellicott, v.9 – see note](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/job/28.htm)

**v. 11 — “He stops up the sources of the streams to bring what is hidden to light.”**

Gill: the miner “bindeth the floods from overflowing” — he dams them up so firmly “that the waters cannot so much as ooze, or distil and drop as a tear from the eye” (the Hebrew root means “weeping”). The “thing that is hid bringeth he forth to light” — the metals and gems that lay hidden in the earth are fetched out by diligence and labour. [Gill, v.11](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/job/28.htm)

The Pulpit Commentary: “The word translated ‘overflowing’ means probably ‘weeping,’ and seems to point to that leakage from the roofs and sides of galleries and adits which is more difficult to control.” The end result is that “things useful or beautiful that are hidden deep down in the heart of the earth … are brought out … into the light of day.” [Pulpit, v.11](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/28.htm)

Ellicott adds that “the canals and cisterns were made so accurately that they retained the water, and did not even weep or trickle.” [Ellicott, v.9 note](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/job/28.htm)

---

## Part 2: The Search for Wisdom (vv.12–19)

**v. 12 — “But where can wisdom be found, and where does understanding dwell?”**

Ellicott: “With magnificent effect comes in this question, after the gigantic achievements of man just recounted; notwithstanding his industry, science, and skill, he is altogether ignorant of true wisdom.” [Ellicott, v.12](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/job/28.htm)

The Pulpit Commentary marks this as the “abrupt change” in the chapter. From human ingenuity Job turns to “wisdom” — “the reason which deals with principles.” Perfect wisdom can only dwell with God (v.23). [Pulpit, v.12](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/28.htm)

Enduring Word: “Job here made the point he had built up to in the previous verses. Men search hard and are willing to endure danger for the sake of the riches of this earth, but all of that is easy compared to the search for wisdom.” [Enduring Word](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-28/)

From Desiring God (John Piper), as captured in the search excerpt: “Job says, ‘Where shall wisdom be found? And where is the place of understanding?’ … He’s listened to his well-meaning, but misguided friends fumble for answers for more than twenty-five chapters.” [Desiring God](https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/secret-wisdom-in-the-wake-of-suffering)

The Pulpit Commentary notes that the Hebrew words for “wisdom” (*chokmah*) and “understanding” (*binah*) may or may not carry a formal distinction; Dean Plumptre suggests the Septuagint’s distinction between *sophia* (scientific knowledge) and *phronesis* (practical intelligence that directs conduct), but “it may be doubted whether Job does not use the two words as synonyms.” [Pulpit, v.12](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/28.htm)

**v. 13 — “No man can know its value, nor is it found in the land of the living.”**

The Pulpit Commentary: “The real value of wisdom cannot be estimated in terms of ordinary human calculation. It transcends figures. … True wisdom … does not exist among men. It transcends human faculties, and is among the peculiar possessions of the Most High (v.23).” [Pulpit, v.13](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/28.htm)

**v. 14 — “The ocean depths say, ‘It is not in me,’ while the sea declares, ‘It is not with me.’”**

The Pulpit Commentary: “The deep abysses of the ocean declare that it is not with them; and the wide reaches of the far-extending sea proclaim that it is not with them either.” Wisdom cannot be located in the natural creation. [Pulpit, v.14](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/28.htm)

Gill: wisdom “is not to be found by sea or land, or among any of the creatures.” [Gill, Introduction](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/job/28.htm)

**v. 15 — “It cannot be bought with gold, nor can its price be weighed out in silver.”**

The Pulpit Commentary: “No amount of gold can purchase it … God must grant it, and find a way of imparting it; which he certainly will not do for a sum of money.” If gold cannot buy it, “much less can silver — the less valuable medium of exchange.” (On weighing silver in ancient sales, see Genesis 23:16.) [Pulpit, v.15](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/28.htm)

Enduring Word, citing Andersen: “The logic of saying in one breath, ‘It isn’t there, but, even if it were, you couldn’t buy it’, is often met in the Bible.” [Enduring Word](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-28/)

**v. 16 — “It cannot be valued in the gold of Ophir, in precious onyx or sapphire.”**

The Pulpit Commentary locates Ophir most probably in south-east Arabia. The “gold of Ophir” was prized because the natural product of those mines surpassed what ancient refining could achieve. The “onyx” is probably the sardonyx, highly prized and found in the high priest’s breastplate (Exodus 28:20) and among the treasures of the King of Tyre (Ezekiel 28:13). [Pulpit, v.16](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/28.htm)

**v. 17 — “Neither gold nor crystal can compare to it, nor jewels of fine gold be exchanged for it.”**

The Pulpit Commentary suggests the patriarch may be thinking of “some goblet or ornament in which crystal and gold were combined together” — such ornaments having been found in Phoenicia. “Vessels of fine gold” were common in both Egypt and Phoenicia. Even these cannot equal wisdom. [Pulpit, v.17](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/28.htm)

Ellicott notes that the Hebrew word rendered “exchange” may also mean “attraction.” [Ellicott, v.17](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/job/28.htm)

**v. 18 — “Coral and quartz are unworthy of mention; the price of wisdom is beyond rubies.”**

The Pulpit Commentary notes that the Hebrew word rendered “coral” (*ra’moth*) literally means “things that are high” and occurs only here and Ezekiel 27:16. The rabbinical interpretation as “coral” is uncertain since the LXX did not know it. The word for “rubies” (*peninim*) is also obscure — rendered variously as rubies, pearls, carbuncles, or red coral, “the balance of authority is in favour of pearls.” [Pulpit, v.18](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/28.htm)

**v. 19 — “Topaz from Cush cannot compare to it, nor can it be valued in pure gold.”**

The Pulpit Commentary: the *pitdah* is either topaz or chrysolite. Pliny’s mention of its green tints favours chrysolite. “Cush” here is probably Cushite Arabia (southern and south-eastern regions), not African Ethiopia. Job uses four different Hebrew words for gold (vv.15–17) — for common gold, treasured gold, native gold from washings/nuggets, and a poetical name for gold of extreme purity — “to show that there was no gold of any kind wherewith it was possible to purchase wisdom.” [Pulpit, v.19](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/28.htm)

---

## Part 3: God Alone Knows Wisdom (vv.20–28)

**v. 20 — “From where then does wisdom come, and where does understanding dwell?”**

This is a near-repetition of v.12. The Pulpit Commentary notes it is a “mere variant of the verb in the first line” — Job’s elaborate inquiry of vv.14–19 having “thrown no light on the subject, the original question recurs.” [Pulpit, v.20](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/28.htm)

Enduring Word: “Job explained how hard it was to find wisdom, and then asked the logical question. Job knew that he needed this precious wisdom, and he certainly knew that his friends needed this wisdom.” [Enduring Word](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-28/)

**v. 21 — “It is hidden from the eyes of every living thing and concealed from the birds of the air.”**

The Pulpit Commentary: “Man cannot see it, because it is immaterial, but he cannot even conceive of it, because its nature transcends him. … The sight of birds is far keener than that of man; but even birds cannot detect where wisdom is.” [Pulpit, v.21](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/28.htm)

From the Desiring God article (search excerpt): “We will not find the right answers in the world — in newspapers, books, schools, or with Google. The world is filled with knowledge, opinion, and passion, but is starving for wisdom.” [Desiring God](https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/secret-wisdom-in-the-wake-of-suffering)

**v. 22 — “Abaddon and Death say, ‘We have heard a rumor about it.’”**

The Pulpit Commentary: “Death and destruction” represent the inhabitants of Sheol — the world of the departed. Job personifies them and represents them as saying “that in their gloomy and remote abode … they have heard some dim rumour, some vague report, of the ‘place’ of wisdom … but their knowledge on the subject does not much transcend the knowledge of living men.” Thus neither the living nor the dead can answer the great question. [Pulpit, v.22](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/28.htm)

Ellicott adds a poignant observation: “That destruction and death should have heard the fame of wisdom is natural, as it consists in departing from the evil which leads to their abode.” [Ellicott, v.22](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/job/28.htm)

**v. 23 — “But God understands its way, and He knows its place.”**

This is the turning point. The Pulpit Commentary: “God only understands what true wisdom is. It is a part of his being, an essential element of his nature. He knows ‘the way’ of it, i.e. how it works and manifests itself; and he knows ‘the place’ of it, i.e. where it dwells.” The highest knowledge is all hidden in God (cf. Colossians 2:3). [Pulpit, v.23](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/28.htm)

Ellicott: “God is the author of wisdom, and His fear is the beginning thereof; so with His infinite knowledge of the universe He cannot but be cognisant of the place and way thereof.” He further observes that “the very existence of wisdom in relation to man implied the existence of evil, because except by departing from evil there could for man be no wisdom.” [Ellicott, v.23](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/job/28.htm)

Enduring Word, quoting G. Campbell Morgan: “This is, indeed, at once our confidence and our comfort — ‘God understandeth.’ The things that perplex us, do not perplex Him; the mysteries by which we are surrounded, are no mysteries to Him.” [Enduring Word](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-28/)

**v. 24 — “For He looks to the ends of the earth and sees everything under the heavens.”**

The Pulpit Commentary contrasts God’s unlimited knowledge with man’s limited knowledge. “Man is conditioned. God is unconditioned. … It is the universality of God’s knowledge that makes each item of it perfect. Where knowledge is circumscribed, it is impossible to be sure that some truth outside the circle … has not a bearing on that which is within.” God alone has no such limits. [Pulpit, v.24](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/28.htm)

**v. 25 — “When God fixed the weight of the wind and measured out the waters…”**

The JFB commentary (from search excerpt): “God has adjusted the weight of the winds, so seemingly imponderable, lest, if too weighty, or too light, injury should be caused. He measureth out the waters, fixing their bounds, with wisdom as His counsellor (Proverbs 8:27–31; Isaiah 40:12).” [JFB, v.25](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/job/28.htm)

The Pulpit Commentary: “God by his wisdom gives to winds their exactly fitting degree of force and violence, so that they perform the work in the world which they were intended to perform … Everything in creation is duly proportioned to every other thing. All is ordered ‘by weight and with care.’” [Pulpit, v.25](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/28.htm)

The Desiring God article (search excerpt) notes how hard this verse would have been for Job to say after losing his children in a great wind (Job 1:19): “He weighs and wields the wind — imagine how hard it would be for Job to say those words after seeing his dead children … God weaved the world with wisdom and runs the world with wisdom, including every drop of rain, every cool summer breeze, and every hurricane-force gust.” [Desiring God](https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/secret-wisdom-in-the-wake-of-suffering)

**v. 26 — “…when He set a limit for the rain and a path for the thunderbolt…”**

The Pulpit Commentary: “God ‘made a decree for the rain’ when he placed the fall of rain under fixed and unalterable laws. … God gave laws to the electric current, and prescribed the ‘way’ that it should take. … Everything was ruled beforehand by Infinite Wisdom.” [Pulpit, v.26](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/28.htm)

**v. 27 — “…then He looked at wisdom and appraised it; He established it and searched it out.”**

Ellicott makes a significant observation about the four verbs used of God’s relationship to wisdom: “(1) seeing, or intuition; (2) declaring or numbering, ratiocination; (3) preparing or establishing, determination; (4) searching out, or investigation. Each of these actions implies the operation of mind, and is so far opposed to the fatality of an impersonal law or the fixed necessity of an inevitable nature.” [Ellicott, v.27](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/job/28.htm)

The Pulpit Commentary notes the curious inverted order (God “prepared” before He “searched out”). The explanation is that “God must first have investigated and searched out, in his own secret counsels, the entire scheme of creation, and afterwards have proceeded to the ‘preparation’ or ‘establishment’ of it.” This is a common biblical inversion for rhetorical effect. [Pulpit, v.27](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/28.htm)

**v. 28 — “And He said to man, ‘Behold, the fear of the Lord, that is wisdom, and to turn away from evil is understanding.’”**

This is the climactic verse. Gill explains that “the fear of the Lord” here means “not a fear of his wrath, and of eternal damnation, but an affection for God with reverence of him; such as is peculiar to children, a godly filial fear … it is not from nature, or in men naturally, but comes from the grace of God, and is a gift of it.” [Gill, v.28](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/job/28.htm)

Ellicott: “No one can for a moment suppose that this is an historical statement … but it is nevertheless profoundly and universally true. It is the wisdom of man as man to fear the Lord and to depart from evil; and this is God’s primary revelation to man.” He also notes that the Hebrew word for “the Lord” here is *Adonai*, not the four-lettered name *Jehovah* (which Job used in 12:9); *Adonai* was “in later times universally substituted for the name Jehovah by the Jews in reading.” [Ellicott, v.28](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/job/28.htm)

The Pulpit Commentary: God spoke this “not in so many words, not by any written or spoken revelation; but by the nature which he implanted in man, and especially by the conscience wherewith he endowed him. Man feels in his heart of hearts that whatever wisdom may be in the abstract, his true wisdom is ‘the fear of God,’ his true understanding ‘to depart from evil.’” [Pulpit, v.28](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/28.htm)

Enduring Word adds Adam Clarke’s insight: this “probably refers to the revelation of his will which God gave to Adam after his fall. He had before sought for wisdom in a forbidden way … Thus they lost all the wisdom that they had, by not setting the fear of the Lord before their eyes … The fear of the Lord, that is wisdom; it is thy only wisdom now to set God always before thy eyes.” [Enduring Word](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-28/)

Enduring Word also notes that the verse connects to Psalm 111:10, Proverbs 9:10, and Proverbs 15:33. “If true wisdom can be simply gained by human effort, energy, and ingenuity (like the rare and precious metals of the earth), then the fear of the Lord is not essential to obtaining wisdom. But if it comes from God’s revelation, then right relationship with Him is the key.” [Enduring Word](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-28/)

The Desiring God article (search excerpt) stresses: “The fear of the Lord is not terror, but awe-filled faith. … ‘The fear of the Lord leads to life, and whoever has it rests satisfied’ (Proverbs 19:23). … If God and his wisdom are our comfort and confidence, we will walk away from foolishness and evil.” [Desiring God](https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/secret-wisdom-in-the-wake-of-suffering)

---

## Differing Protestant Traditions

**Who speaks chapter 28?** This is the main area where commentators divide.

- **Traditional/Conservative (most older commentators, Gill, Henry, Grant, Garner-Howes Baptist):** The chapter is Job’s own speech. Gill treats it as Job’s unified discourse throughout. Grant’s Commentary states: “Job discerned this, though men generally have no regard for this simple yet profound pronouncement.” [Grant, v.28](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/lmg/job-28.html)

- **Some modern evangelical scholars:** The chapter is the narrator’s interlude. Enduring Word reports Andersen’s view: “Because we think that Job is a story, we find it appropriate that this interlude is spoken by the story-teller. It sums up the case as it stands at this point. It … lays the foundation for [the Lord’s speeches] by showing their necessity.” [Enduring Word](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-28/)

- **Coffman’s Commentary (broadly evangelical/Church of Christ):** Rejects the “choral interlude” theory: “The theory that this is a choral ode not closely related to Job is unacceptable, because what has disturbed Job throughout the book is the incomprehensible nature of God’s wisdom.” Also rejects assigning the chapter to Zophar. [Coffman](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/job-28.html)

**On “the fear of the Lord” (v.28):**

- **Baptist (Garner-Howes):** Emphasises that Job infers his friends “could have that wisdom and understanding if they would seek it from the Lord (*Adonai* or master) instead of trying to fix imagined evil on him.” Also cites James 1:5 — wisdom is to be asked of God who gives liberally. [Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary, v.28](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/job-28.html)

- **Reformed Baptist (John Piper/Desiring God):** Stresses the hiddenness of God’s wisdom in suffering and the need for awe-filled trust, not terror. “We cannot capture or completely grasp his wisdom, but we can worship him and trust him with all the painful unknowns in life.” [Desiring God](https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/secret-wisdom-in-the-wake-of-suffering)

- **Pentecostal/Charismatic (Enduring Word, David Guzik):** Emphasises that “the gaining of wisdom requires the total sacrifice of our single most precious possession: ourselves. More specifically, what is required is the surrender of our wills” (quoting Mason). This personal-surrender emphasis is characteristic of broadly Pentecostal devotional reading. [Enduring Word](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-28/)

- **Brethren/Dispensational (Grant):** “The only reason that wisdom eludes people is that ‘there is no fear of God before their eyes,’ so that they have no heart to depart from evil.” [Grant, v.28](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/lmg/job-28.html)

- **Anglican (Ellicott):** Notes the finer philological points (e.g., *Adonai* not *Jehovah* in v.28). Draws a broader canonical connection: though the wisdom of Job 28:28 “is in no way connected with the Gospel of the kingdom … it is impossible not to recognise a central thought underlying all such words … from the one Shepherd.” He connects it to the evangelical promises of Isaiah (Isaiah 55:1) and Christ’s parable of the pearl of great price. [Ellicott, vv.23, 28](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/job/28.htm)
